parte: Part I · Why accounting looks the way it does
titlu: The Drawers: The Chart of Accounts

blocuri.text: The previous chapter ended with a practical question. If every amount is recorded in two places, which places exactly? Goods in one, the debt owed to the supplier in another, revenue in a third. These places are called accounts, and their complete list is the chart of accounts.

This is probably the page that looks scariest at first glance: several hundred lines of figures. The good news is that it isn't meant to be memorized, and the best news is that the logic behind it can be explained in a quarter of an hour. After that, the chart is read, not memorized.
What an Account Actually Is
An account is a card that gathers, in one place, all movements of the same kind. The card has exactly two columns — the ones from the previous chapter: left, debit; right, credit. That's it.

The card for account "Cash in lei" gathers everything that came in and everything that went out of the cash register. The card for account "Suppliers" gathers everything you came to owe and everything you paid. At any moment, the difference between the two columns is called the balance and answers a precise question: how much do I have in cash right now, how much do I still owe suppliers.

An account, then, is not an administrative file. It's a question you want to be able to answer at any time, without digging through invoices. The number of accounts in a chart is the number of questions the legislator considered worth being able to ask separately.
Eight Families, in a Logical Order

The Romanian chart of accounts is not an alphabetical list, but a classification. The first digit of any account tells you which family it belongs to, and the families are arranged in an order that is not accidental.

blocuri.titlu: Classes of the Chart of Accounts
randuri: Equity — what the business owner put in and what has accumulated over time
Fixed Assets — goods that serve for several years
Inventory — goods that are consumed or sold
Third Parties — who owes you and whom you owe
Expenses — what was consumed during the period
Revenue — what was earned during the period
Special Accounts — what isn't yours, but concerns you
blocuri.nota: Classes 1–5 answer the book's second question (what do I have and what do I owe). Classes 6 and 7 answer the first (how much have I earned).

blocuri.text: The order of classes 1–5 follows a principle: from what is most stable to what is most liquid. Capital stays put for years; a building, for many years; goods, for a few months; a receivable, a few weeks; money in the account is already money. Whoever goes through classes 1 to 5 is, in effect, descending the slope of time.
Classes 1–5 are the balance sheet. Classes 6 and 7 are the income statement. The two documents from Chapter 1 are, literally, two slices of the same chart.
The Difference That Only Shows at Year-End
Between the first five classes and the next two there is a difference of nature, not of content, and it's worth understanding early, because it explains half of the operations at year-end closing.

An account from classes 1–5 has memory. The cash balance on December 31 becomes the cash balance on January 1; the money doesn't disappear because the year changed. The same goes for receivables, liabilities, inventory.

An account from classes 6 and 7 has no memory, and shouldn't have any. The question "how much have I spent" only makes sense if you specify for how long — otherwise you keep adding forever. That's why, at the end of each year, all revenue and expense accounts are emptied into a single account, 121 Profit or Loss, and the following year they start from zero. This operation has a chapter of its own further ahead; for now, it's enough to note that the emptying isn't a formality, but the natural consequence of the fact that it measures a period.
How to Read a Code
The digits are not inventory numbers, but an address that is read from left to right, narrowing the meaning at each step.

blocuri.titlu: The Same Address, Read Step by Step
randuri: third-party accounts — someone owes me or I owe someone
a specific customer, opened by the company
blocuri.nota: The first four levels are fixed by regulation and are the same for all companies in the country. The fifth is opened by the company, if it needs to.

blocuri.text: The uniformity of the first levels is why the accounting of two companies can be compared, and a trial balance can be read by anyone in the profession. It's not bureaucracy: it's like postal addresses, where the street is written the same way for everyone, otherwise the letter never arrives.
Which Side an Account Increases On
The previous chapter said that debit and credit don't mean plus and minus, but left and right, and that the effect depends on the account. Now we can say precisely what it depends on: the class.

randuri: What you have (classes 2, 3, 5 and receivables from 4)
What you owe and what you earn (classes 1, 7 and liabilities from 4)
blocuri.nota: There are also accounts that work in both directions, called dual-function accounts — 121 Profit or Loss is the best known: it has a credit balance for profit and a debit balance for loss.

blocuri.text: The rule is easier to remember starting from a single observation: accounting looks at things from the company's perspective, not yours. When the bank tells you "we have credited your account," it's speaking from its own perspective — for the bank, you are a liability. In your company's accounting, that same money coming in increases the bank account on the debit side.
Analytical Accounts: The Only Part You Choose Yourself

Account 4111 gathers all customers together. That's enough to know how much you have to collect in total, but it doesn't tell you from whom. For that, analytical accounts are opened — 4111.01, 4111.02, and so on, one per customer.

The practical rule is simple: open an analytical account only where you really need a separate answer. A chart with a thousand unnecessary analytical accounts is harder to read than one with twenty well-chosen ones, and at the end of the month someone still has to review them.

In practice, an accounting program keeps records per partner without forcing you to open anything; analytical accounts remain for cases where you want the separation to appear right in the trial balance.

The general chart of accounts is established by accounting regulations (OMFP 1802/2014) and its structure is mandatory: the symbol and name of first- and second-degree synthetic accounts cannot be changed, only analytical accounts can be added. Class 8 comprises off-balance-sheet accounts, with their own accounting function (they do not enter the balance sheet equation), and class 9 — management accounting — is optional and, in small companies, generally unused; the chart in the application does not contain it at all. The function of each account (asset, liability, or dual-function) is the one set out in the regulations and determines the side on which increases are recorded; apparent exceptions — corrective accounts such as 129 Profit Distribution, or the adjustments in groups 29, 39, 49, 59 — do not contradict the rule, but rather correct another account, which is why they function in reverse relative to the account they correct. When opening an analytical account, take care that the sum of the analytical balances remains equal to the synthetic balance: a mismatch between them is one of the most common causes of a trial balance that "won't close" when taking over a company.
Why You Don't Need to Memorize It

A business owner never opens the chart of accounts. In an accounting program, they say what document they have — a supplier invoice, a receipt, a bank statement — and the program chooses the drawers. That choice is called the accounting mapping, and it is, essentially, a dictionary between everyday language and the language of accounts.

An accountant does open it, but not to memorize it: to verify. When a figure looks odd in a report, the way back invariably passes through an account's card, and from there through the document that produced it. The chart is the map on which that journey is made.

With that, the tools are on the table: we know what questions accounting answers, why every amount is recorded twice, and exactly where it is recorded. One question remains, which is not technical but everything hinges on it: who is responsible for these figures. That is the subject of the next chapter.
How to Read an Account You've Never Seen Before
No one memorizes the chart of accounts. It is read, and reading it involves three steps that work for any symbol, including one encountered for the first time.

blocuri.titlu: The Three Questions, Applied to an Example: Account 4426
randuri: 4 — third-party accounts: a relationship with someone outside
4426 — deductible VAT, tax paid to suppliers
blocuri.nota: The more digits you add, the more precise the question becomes. The general meaning, however, is read from the first digit.

blocuri.text: The three levels have names in the regulation: first-degree synthetic account (three digits), second-degree synthetic account (four digits), and analytical account (whatever is added afterward, at the company's choice). An analytical account is not a new account — it is a breakdown of the synthetic one, and the sum of all analytical accounts must equal exactly the balance of the synthetic account.
The Second Digit, Which Tells You the Meaning

There is a pattern that shortens learning considerably, and textbooks often pass over it in silence. In fixed asset and inventory accounts, an 8 in the second position means depreciation, and a 9 means impairment adjustment. These are corrective accounts: they don't add value, they subtract it.

blocuri.titlu: The Base Account and Its Corrective Accounts
randuri: how much of it has been consumed
how much of the remaining value is likely lost
blocuri.nota: On the balance sheet, only a single figure appears: net value, i.e., 213 minus 281 minus 291. The three accounts exist so it can be shown what that figure is made of.

enunt: Without looking it up in the chart, say what kind of account each of these is and on which side its balance normally sits: 401, 5121, 607, 707, 4423, 1012, 2813.
Hint: the first digit gives the class; classes 1, 4 (partially) and 7 are generally credit accounts, classes 2, 3, 5 and 6 are debit accounts.
rezolvare: 401 — class 4, third parties: liability toward suppliers, credit balance.
5121 — class 5, treasury: money in the account, debit balance.
607 — class 6, expenses: cost of goods sold, debit balance.
707 — class 7, revenue: sales of goods, credit balance.
4423 — class 4: VAT payable, liability toward the budget, credit balance.
1012 — class 1, equity: shareholders' contribution, credit balance.
2813 — class 2 with an 8 in the second position: depreciation of vehicles, a CORRECTIVE account, credit balance even though it belongs to the asset class.
The last one is the only one that requires attention, and it's exactly the pattern from the previous section: an 8 in the second position means the balance is subtracted, not added.

puncte: An account is a card with two columns that gathers movements of the same kind; the difference between the columns is the balance.
The first digit gives the class. Classes 1–5 form the balance sheet, classes 6 and 7 the income statement.
Accounts 1–5 carry their balance forward from one year to the next; revenue and expense accounts are emptied annually into 121, because they measure a period.
The code is read like an address: class, group, first- and second-degree synthetic accounts — fixed by law — then the analytical account, opened by the company.
What you have increases on the debit side; what you owe and what you earn increase on the credit side. Apparent exceptions are corrective accounts.
The chart is not learned by heart: it is read whenever you're checking a figure.
